titolo: The Extreme Geography Behind The Richest Countries On Earth
descrizione:
Good land should make a country rich. So why are some of the richest nations on Earth frozen, dry, flooded, jungle-covered, or almost out of land? We look at eight countries where terrible geography turned into the money itself.

From Australian iron and Icelandic volcanoes to Dutch dikes, Guyana's oil, Qatar's gas, Norway's fund, Luxembourg's finance and Singapore's strait, we follow the maps, the numbers and the surprising stories behind each fortune.

scene.testo: A country that earned less than Ecuador. A gas giant that lost a sixth of its exports in two days. And the richest place has almost no land.
How do the worst places on Earth become the richest?
If good land made countries rich, the richest places would be green and gentle, with deep soil, big rivers and mild weather.
But look where the money actually is: a frozen coast, a desert with no rivers, a jungle, and land below the sea.
And one island was so short of land that it had to build more of itself. These are eight of the richest countries on Earth.
Here is the strange part. The terrible geography is not what they overcame. It is where the money came from.
Number eight. In 1938, Australia banned the export of its own iron ore, believing it simply did not have enough.
In truth it sat on one of the biggest iron deposits on Earth. The problem was the land on top.
Australia is the driest inhabited continent, and its ten biggest deserts alone cover eighteen percent of the mainland.
Under that empty interior lies rock more than three billion years old, where iron built up into whole mountains of ore.
In 1952, rancher Lang Hancock, forced by bad weather to fly low through a Pilbara gorge, saw walls of rust-red iron.

scene.testo: The export ban ended in 1960, and mines opened soon after. Today, iron ore is Australia's biggest export, worth 116 billion Australian dollars in a year.
Australia ships over half of all iron ore traded worldwide, and about eighty-five percent of it goes to one customer: China.
The desert was never the problem. It was the vault. Adjusted for prices, that is about 75,000 dollars for every Australian.
Some of what Australia digs up travels north. And one island makes aluminum without a single aluminum mine. Number seven: Iceland.
Every year ships bring in alumina, the white powder aluminum is made from, from as far as Australia and Brazil.
Why haul it so far? Because of what sits under Iceland: over thirty active volcanic systems, and glaciers covering a tenth of the country.
Glacier meltwater spins its hydro plants, and volcanic heat drives its geothermal ones. Together they make almost all of Iceland's electricity.
That is far more power than 394,000 people need. So Iceland exports it in the one form a ship can carry: melted into metal.
Each ingot leaving Iceland is Icelandic electricity in solid form. In 2025, aluminum was about a third of all goods Iceland sold abroad.
Isolation gave Iceland something else: the sea. It fought Britain three times over fishing waters and, in 1975, pushed its limit to 200 miles.
Fish is still its biggest goods export, just ahead of aluminum. Per person, that is around 83,000 dollars, ahead of the United States.
Number six comes with a number you have probably heard wrong. People say over half the Netherlands lies below sea level. Even a UN report printed it.
The real figure is about a quarter. But almost sixty percent of the country could flood, from the sea or from its rivers.
So why build a rich country here? Because this soggy corner is where three rivers reach the sea: the Rhine, the Meuse and the Scheldt.
The Rhine runs straight into the industrial heart of Europe. Whoever holds the river mouth holds the trade. That is Rotterdam.
Rotterdam is Europe's biggest port, handling about one in every eight tons of cargo moving through EU ports.
Holding back the sea also forced people to cooperate. Dutch water boards go back to the 1200s, among the oldest democratic bodies in the country.
In 1953, the sea broke through anyway and killed more than 1,800 people. The Dutch answered with the Delta Works, a giant wall of dams and storm barriers.
The land won from the sea became a food machine. In 2025, Dutch agricultural exports hit a record 137 billion euros, counting goods passing through its ports.
In the 1600s, the Dutch Republic was likely the richest place on Earth per person, for the same reason: everything flowed through its water.
Today the Netherlands sits at about 88,000 dollars per person. Quick favor: these videos take long to make, so if you enjoy this one, subscribing helps.
The Dutch took their dikes across the Atlantic. On a swampy South American coast, planters forced enslaved Africans to dig dikes, canals and polders.
That colony is number five: Guyana. In 2015, the average Guyanese earned less than the average person in Ecuador or Colombia.
Today, adjusted for prices, Guyana earns more per person than the United States.
Most of Guyana is rainforest. Nine in ten people live on a thin coastal strip, and the capital, Georgetown, sits below high tide behind a seawall.
The jungle kept the country empty and poor. Then, in May 2015, ExxonMobil drilled off that coast and found a huge oil field.
The first oil flowed in December 2019. Now Guyana pumps around 900,000 barrels a day for only about a million people.
In 2022, its economy grew sixty-two percent in a single year, the fastest in the world.
Here is what almost nobody mentions: the jungle pays, too. In 2022, Guyana became the first country to issue a carbon credit for forest it does not cut.
The oil company Hess agreed to buy at least 750 million dollars of them. The forest that kept Guyana poor is now paid to stand still.
There is one catch. Venezuela claims about two thirds of the country, and the World Court's ruling is expected within months.
Number four shares the biggest gas field on Earth with Iran, and earns about eighteen times more per person. This is Qatar.
It has no rivers, and under two percent of it is farmland. Almost all tap water comes from desalination, and the record heat tops fifty degrees Celsius.
For centuries, the main money was under the water: men diving for pearls. Then, around 1930, Japan began selling cheap cultured pearls.
The Great Depression hit, the pearl trade collapsed, and Qatar sank into decades of hardship. Whole families packed up and left.
Later came something far bigger under Qatar's own sea, the North Field. But it does not stop at the border: it runs into Iran, which calls it South Pars.
Qatar chilled its gas into liquid and shipped it worldwide. In 2024, it supplied almost a fifth of all liquefied natural gas traded on Earth.
There are not many Qataris to share it. Only about one resident in nine is a citizen.
But this year, the geography that made Qatar rich turned on it. Every tanker must squeeze through one narrow gate, the Strait of Hormuz.
In March, during the war with Iran, missiles hit Ras Laffan, the heart of Qatar's gas industry. Qatar Energy says it lost about seventeen percent of export capacity.
That is roughly 20 billion dollars a year, and repairs could take three to five years. Even now, income is around 104,000 per head, adjusted for prices.
In 1969, Phillips Petroleum was about to give up on Norway. Its North Sea wells kept coming up dry.
It drilled one last well, mainly because it was stuck with a hired rig and drilling cost less than walking away. That well found Ekofisk.
The first giant oil field in Western Europe turned number three, Norway, into an oil country, on a frozen, rocky coast that held one more gift.
Its mountains and all that rain give Norway hydropower for almost nine tenths of its electricity. So it barely burns its own oil and gas, and sells almost all of it.
In 2025, Norwegian gas covered more than thirty percent of what the EU and Britain used.
Even the fjords played a part. Troll A, a gas platform 472 meters tall, was built in one piece and towed out to sea in 1995.
It is the tallest structure humans have ever moved. And the money was not spent. It was saved.
Norway's oil fund is worth about 23 trillion kroner, around 4 million for every Norwegian, and it owns about one and a half percent of every listed company on Earth.
A cold, rocky edge of Europe built the largest national savings fund on Earth. Per Norwegian, about 116,000 dollars.
Every morning, more than 200,000 people cross into number two from France, Germany and Belgium. Every evening, they go home.
Almost half of everyone who works in Luxembourg lives in another country. It is smaller than Rhode Island, with no coast, squeezed between three neighbors.
Under its southern hills lay iron ore so full of phosphorus it was almost useless, until a new British steel method in 1879 made it workable.
Luxembourg became a steel country. When the ore ran out and European steel crashed, it turned to finance.
Today, more than 8 trillion euros in investment funds are based in Luxembourg, more than anywhere except the United States. That gives about 157,000 per resident.
But remember those commuters? They help produce the income, yet they do not count as residents. So the figure per person is inflated.
In 1965, Malaysia voted number one out of its federation. On the ninth of August, it was on its own.
Its central bank described what it had: an island of about 580 square kilometers, no resources, no hinterland, and not even enough water.
What it had was a spot on the map. Singapore sits at the end of the Strait of Malacca, the busiest oil choke point on Earth.
So it built a port. Last year it handled a record 44.7 million containers, second only to Shanghai.
It had no land, so it made some. Singapore is now about a quarter bigger than in 1965, built out into the sea with imported sand.
By the UN's count, it became the world's biggest importer of sand. It also had no water, so it buys some from Malaysia under a deal that runs until 2061.
And it recycles its own sewage into water clean enough to drink. In 1965, a Singaporean earned about 500 dollars, against 300 for a Malaysian.
Today, a Singaporean earns almost seven times more than a Malaysian: almost 177,000 dollars per person, the highest of any country with over a million people.
Eight of the worst places to build a country, and in almost every one, the handicap turned into the money.
Treasure under the handicap: Australia, Guyana, Qatar and Norway. Location over land: the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Singapore. The handicap as a power plant: Iceland.
And the handicap that forced them to get good: the Dutch against the sea, Singapore against having no land or water. Most also share very few people to split the money between.
Qatar got rich behind a strait. Singapore got rich by sitting on one. And the richest country in the world is not even on this list.

Liechtenstein beats all eight, and its money has almost nothing to do with geography. Its neighbor Switzerland is the purest version of this story, with no sea, no oil, nothing to dig, and still among the richest on Earth.
The countries that got rich did not escape their geography. They found the price tag hidden inside it.
